title: World Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya, SoftBank Plunges 16% in Asian Tech Sell-Off, and Japan Core Inflation Hits Yearly High
subhead: The International Court of Justice delivers a landmark genocide verdict against Myanmar as Asian tech stocks tumble following Anthropic's IPO debut, Japan's core inflation accelerates after energy subsidies expire, and Russian strikes hit embassies in Kyiv.

sections.heading: World Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
sections.body:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that the state of Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during the 2017 military crackdown, marking the first time the United Nations' top court has held a state directly culpable for genocide, the New York Times reports. The judgment carries broad legal implications for international accountability and refugee protections across South and Southeast Asia.

In neighboring Thailand and across regional capitals, governments now face renewed diplomatic pressure over cross-border displacement and Myanmar's military leadership, coming a day after junta chief Min Aung Hlaing threatened to review Myanmar's ties with ASEAN over perceived 'indignity.' Meanwhile, in Europe, France 24 notes Kamala Harris is scheduled to meet French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris on Friday in a courtesy visit closely watched for 2028 US political positioning.
sections.whyItMatters: A formal ICJ genocide finding against a sitting state establishes a high-profile international legal precedent that raises diplomatic and sanctions exposure for Myanmar's military rulers and their external backers.

sections.heading: SoftBank Plunges 16% as AI Sell-Off Rocks Asian Equities After Anthropic Debut
sections.body:
Asian technology equities slumped sharply on Friday, with SoftBank Group shares plunging more than 16% as investors rotated out of high-multiple AI names following Anthropic's volatile Nasdaq debut, CNBC and CNA report. Asian markets were on track for their worst weekly drop since 2020, while Bloomberg notes emerging-market stocks neared bear-market territory under the weight of the AI-led sell-off.

At the same time, CNBC notes analysts called Anthropic's listing 'what the markets need' while warning of near-term share volatility, and the Wall Street Journal reports former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang broke his silence to signal willingness to return to the chipmaker even as SEC and congressional scrutiny intensify. In Hong Kong, SCMP reports brokerage Financial Street Securities confirmed its chairman Zhu Yanhui has been detained by mainland authorities under investigation.
sections.whyItMatters: SoftBank's 16% drop and broader Asian tech selling reveal fragile investor conviction behind trillion-dollar AI valuations, turning Anthropic's post-IPO trading into a bellwether for global equity risk appetite.

sections.heading: Japan Core Inflation Hits Yearly High as Energy Subsidies Expire
sections.body:
Japan's core consumer inflation accelerated in October to its highest level of the year after government energy subsidies expired and pushed up household utility costs, CNBC reports, though the reading came in slightly below the 2.3% consensus forecast by Reuters-polled economists. The rebound complicates the Bank of Japan's rate-normalization path at a moment when Japan's economy already contracted in the third quarter.

In Tokyo's corporate sector, CNA reports government officials assured markets that Japan Tobacco's dividend cut will not disrupt Tokyo's broader industrial investment plans. Separately, oil prices edged higher on Friday after Houthi attacks on Riyadh heightened supply concerns across Gulf energy corridors, CNA writes.
sections.whyItMatters: Subsidy-driven inflation returning in Japan forces Tokyo to balance household cost-of-living pressures against tighter monetary expectations and slowing industrial growth.

sections.heading: Russian Strikes Hit Embassies in Kyiv as Merz Floats Neutral-Ground Talks
sections.body:
Daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged a historic cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands, SCMP reports. On the diplomatic track, Axios reports President Donald Trump called into his envoys' Berlin meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders from Air Force One to insist that Vladimir Putin 'wants to end the war.'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said fresh Ukraine peace talks including European representatives could take place 'soon' on neutral ground, DW reports, as European governments push for a direct seat at the table alongside Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv. Meanwhile, the New York Times writes that despite Trump calling Putin his 'friend' in Shenzhen, the trilateral China-US-Russia summit produced little concrete progress.
sections.whyItMatters: Strikes damaging European embassies in Kyiv underscore the gap between Trump's optimism over Putin's intentions and Europe's demand for enforceable security guarantees before any settlement.

sections.heading: White House Taps Kirsten Davies as Cyber Chief After Outage Wave
sections.body:
The White House moved to replace its top cyber official after a week of disruptive US infrastructure outages, firing National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross and tapping Pentagon official Kirsten Davies to take over, Le Monde, France 24, and The Guardian report. The shake-up follows disruptions across US aviation, banking access, and a classified National Security Agency communications network.

In US politics, NBC News and The Guardian report the Justice Department asked a federal court to dismiss its lawsuit challenging Alaska's US Senate election after Democrat Mary Peltola won the seat. Elsewhere, BBC reports Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI topped $2 billion in estimated launch sales, while South Korea completed its nine-hour Suneung university entrance exam under strict anti-AI cheating controls, CNA reports.
sections.whyItMatters: Replacing the national cyber director mid-crisis signals acute White House concern over recurring systemic outages, even as DOJ drops its Alaska election challenge ahead of the new Senate session.

bottomLine: The World Court's genocide ruling against Myanmar and a 16% slide in SoftBank highlight two simultaneous pressures: hardening international legal accountability and fragile global equity sentiment after Anthropic's debut. With European embassies hit in Kyiv, energy inflation returning in Japan, and a cyber leadership shake-up in Washington, major capitals are navigating acute security and market volatility without clear diplomatic breakthroughs.
sources: New York Times, CNBC, CNA, Bloomberg, SCMP, Axios, DW, Le Monde, France 24, The Guardian, NBC News, BBC
